# Match information (intel)

The pure rules behind §2's timed reveals, §3's rumors and journal, §5's final-island announcement and §11's comeback leads. `@pirate-sea-race/simulation/intel` has the config, the state, `stepIntel`, `targetedRumorAvailability`, `freeCoverage`, `replayIntel` and the three lead phases (`gatherLeads`, `decideLeads`, `answerRequests`). `@pirate-sea-race/content/intel` has the constants and the zod validator `validateIntelRules`. The module doesn't import the ledger. It is integer data with no clocks and no `Math.random`, and time is the world tick (20 per second). `objectives-endgame` wires it into `MatchRoom`; nothing calls it yet.

## Constants (`intelRules`)

| Rule | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Sector grid | 3 × 3, named row by row from "North-West Reach" to "South-East Reach" |
| Sighting delay | 600 ticks (30 s), equal to the carrier interval |
| Carrier interval | 600 ticks (30 s) |
| Sector reveal | 24,000 ticks (minute 20) after control start |
| Carrier reveal | 33,600 ticks (minute 28) after control start |
| Targeted rumor price | 25 gold (the caller charges it) |

The validator refuses a zero interval, reveals out of order, a carrier reveal that isn't a multiple of the interval, a delay that differs from the interval, and names that are missing or repeated. Because the carrier reveal is a multiple of the interval, every broadcast falls on a snapshot boundary, so pending and new sightings can't split across messages.

## Sectors

`sectorOfTile` cuts the map's columns and rows into three bands each by integer division (`floor(tile × 3 / width)`). Every tile is in exactly one sector, and bands differ by at most one tile. On the 224 × 208 slice sea, the columns start at tiles 0, 75 and 150 and the rows at 0, 70 and 139. `sectorOf(position)` is the sector of the position's tile. A position off the map counts in the nearest edge sector. The config computes all of this from the map size, so the same code serves the slice and the 12-island alpha.

## Leads

A rumor names a missing type and a target: an **island**, where a source of that type is still sealed, or a **sector**, where a recovery cache holds one. It never names a rubbing, a player or a position. It picks among the eligible targets, sorted, with the seeded generator (`random.ts`) keyed by (seed, tick, player, type), so the same seed gives the same rumor and no other decision changes it. It tries three tiers in order:

1. the islands with a sealed source of the type;
2. the sectors with a cached copy;
3. a **carrier sighting**, and only when every copy of the type is carried by someone else.

Targets already active in the player's journal are skipped, so a player is never given the same lead twice.

Leads are made on four occasions:

- a **start** rumor for each player at control start, or when a player is first seen after it. It only ever names a source or a cache, of any type the player lacks. When every copy of every missing type is carried (a late joiner, say), there is no starting rumor, only a `no-lead`: a start never becomes a carrier sighting;
- a free **fresh** rumor for each type a player lost (§11);
- a **targeted** rumor, bought on request;
- a **replacement**, when a journal rumor goes stale.

Losses and completions come from diffing each player's held types between ticks. A rubbing reserved in a duel still counts as held, so entering a duel is never a loss; only a settled theft is.

**Journal rumors** (island or sector) are the only leads tracked:

- A rumor goes **stale** when its target no longer holds its type: the source was collected or the cache claimed by someone else. The player gets `rumor-stale` with the tick and then a replacement.
- A rumor whose type the holder obtains, by any means, is **resolved** quietly. It gets no replacement.

**Carrier sightings** are one-shot messages, never tracked, so they can never go stale and can't be used to follow a carrier. At every carrier boundary (control start plus a multiple of 30 s, counted when crossed), the state takes one snapshot of the carried copies: the sector, the type and the internal holder of each. It keeps the latest two. A sighting reads the **older** of the two, so it is 30–60 s old and never the current position. It also skips the requester's own former entries.

Only three triggers ask for a sighting: a loss (`fresh`), a journal replacement and a targeted request. The sighting's reason type (`CarrierSightingReason`) has only these three, so a start can't produce one. A `carrier-sighting` message may list several types: one entry per type (the type, the trigger's reason and a sector), all from the same older snapshot. Before minute 28, a player gets at most **one sighting message per snapshot**, and at any time at most **one per step**.

**Three phases per step.** Every step builds its lead decisions the same way, whatever order the triggers, the requests or the view's arrays come in:

1. **Gather.** Every trigger joins a set keyed by **(player, type)**: a type lost, a stale rumor's replacement, a pending type at a boundary (the pending set is decided again there), a targeted request. An entry keeps one free trigger (the earliest, then `fresh` before `replacement`) and its request ids, sorted. A pending type the player holds a live journal rumor for (bought since it was deferred) is **dropped** at the boundary instead, quietly: no sighting and no `no-lead`.
2. **Decide.** Per player by id: a starting rumor first (a source or a cache, never a sighting), then each entry in type order. An entry with only requests that free coverage holds for (below) gets nothing sent. Otherwise an entry gets a journal rumor, a `no-lead` (free triggers only), or its type joins the player's one sighting decision. Uncapped (no sighting yet in this snapshot, or minute 28 on), one message lists every such type the older snapshot shows another player carrying; capped, nothing is sent and the free types join the one pending set (a paid type is never queued). A free type the snapshot can't answer yet also waits. Each draw uses a generator keyed by (seed, tick, player, type), and a sighting's sector by (seed, snapshot tick, player, type) among the sorted candidate sectors, so no decision depends on another.
3. **Answer.** Each (player, type)'s requests, by request id (`answerRequests`):
   - `covered` (not charged) when a free trigger or the start already gave the player that type in this step, as a rumor or in the sighting message, or when free coverage holds;
   - otherwise `rumor` or `sighting` for the first request, and `covered` for the rest;
   - when nothing is delivered for that (player, type), every request gets the same `capped` or `none`.

A type goes out with its free trigger's reason if it has one, otherwise `targeted`. So a player who loses two types on one tick, or at a boundary with a type already pending, or loses one while buying another, learns about all of them in one message, and a purchase is never charged for what the step gives for free. Skipped ticks change nothing: two losses seen in one batched view make one message. Two players' requests never affect each other.

**Free coverage.** `freeCoverage(config, state, view, playerId, type)` is the one predicate the step (phase 2, answered in phase 3) and the UI (`targetedRumorAvailability`) share, so they can't disagree. It is `covered` when the type's only eligible target is a carrier, by the same eligibility rumor generation uses (sources, then caches, then carriers), and either:

- **(a)** the minute-28 reveal has happened (on its tick or later): the free 30 s broadcast is fresher than any paid sighting, which reads the older snapshot; or
- **(b)** the type is in the player's pending set after gather (no boundary crossed in this step) and still carrier-only: the next boundary gives it free.

Otherwise it is null and the request is decided as before. With a source or cache target a purchase is a charged `rumor`, even for a pending type (whose pending entry is then dropped at the next boundary) and after minute 28. Players never pay for what they already know or would get free.

**Targeted requests** are `{ requestId, playerId, type }`, and each gets exactly one outcome, whatever the order of the batch:

- `rumor` or `sighting`: something was delivered. Charge the 25 gold only for these two.
- `covered`: this step already gives the player that type, for free or to a request of the same type lower by id, or free coverage holds (nothing is sent). Not charged.
- `capped`: the player already got a sighting in this snapshot (before this step).
- `none`: nothing to sell. The player holds the type, or the player is unknown, or it is before control start, or no untracked target exists.
- `duplicate`: the request id was seen before, or is listed twice in one batch (only its lowest (player, type) is taken). The step answers it without changing the state or drawing from the generator.

`targetedRumorAvailability(config, state, view, playerId, type)` gives the same answer without drawing (`covered` when `freeCoverage` holds), so the UI can show whether buying would yield anything. A later step can differ only if it crosses a snapshot boundary first, or answer `covered` when a free trigger of that player and type in the same step gives the type anyway.

## Reveals (§2, §5)

All reveals fire when their tick is crossed since the last processed tick, so a skipped tick never loses one. Nothing is sent before control start.

- **First full set:** the first player to hold every type of the preset triggers `final-sector` (the final island's sector) to everyone. Each holder of a full set gets `final-route` with the exact point: the first completer, later completers, and anyone who restores a broken set (with `restored: true`). A player who loses a type gets `final-route-inactive`.
- **Minute 20:** `sector-reveal` to everyone, listing the sectors with sealed sources and the sectors with caches.
- **Minute 28, then every 30 s:** `carrier-report` to everyone, listing the (sector, type) pairs of the newest snapshot. Skipping several beats sends one report.
- **Minute 35** belongs to the claim code.

## Messages and hidden information (§16)

`stepIntel(config, state, view, requests) → { state, messages, outcomes }` never writes into its input. Each message is `{ to, body }`, where `to` is `{ kind: "player", playerId }`, `{ kind: "players", playerIds }` or `{ kind: "everyone" }`. Broadcasts are `final-sector`, `sector-reveal` and `carrier-report`; every other kind goes to one player.

Bodies carry sectors, island indexes and names, types, ticks and journal entry numbers. They never carry a player id, a rubbing id, or a source's, cache's or ship's position. The one exact position ever sent is the final island's, in a `final-route` to a full-set holder. The property tests check every message of every run against these rules:

- six seeded runs with compressed reveal times;
- one slice run with the real constants for 36,660 ticks;
- one alpha run with the real constants that skips ticks.

The same runs also check, after every step, that each player got at most one sighting message in it, that every free trigger needing a sighting (a loss, or a stale rumor's replacement) is either in that step's message or in the pending set, and that it waits only if the player's sighting was already spent in this snapshot or the older snapshot shows no other carrier of it. They also check that each player has at most one pending sighting message and that every deferred type goes out at the first boundary after it was capped (or is dropped only when the checker finds it ineligible, or kept only when the previous snapshot shows no other carrier of it). Every rumor is checked against the preference: a cache lead only when no sealed source of the type is left outside the player's journal, a carrier sighting only when no source or cache of the type exists. Every sighting's reason is checked to be `fresh`, `targeted` or `replacement`. Per step and (player, type), at most one request is charged, only when the one lead of that type sent to the player has the reason `targeted` (every lead per (player, type) is kept, so a second, charged lead for a covered type fails). A `covered` request has a lead of its type in that step or free coverage, which the checker derives from the view on its own; a request under free coverage is always `covered`. A black-box check replays the compressed runs, with extra purchases added, against the same script with each step's requests and view arrays shuffled, and compares the messages, the outcomes sorted by request id and `hashState`. Their `EXERCISED` check asserts that every message kind, outcome and lead path occurred, including a deferred delivery, a free trigger sighted in its own step, a message with several types and both kinds of free coverage.

## Building the world view from the ledger

On each processed tick, the caller passes `{ tick, players, rubbings }`:

- **`players`:** each player still in the match (`status` not `left`), with the ship's position in sub-units.
- **`rubbings`:** each ledger rubbing with its `type` and its `location` resolved to a place:
  - `source` becomes `{ kind: "source", island, x, y }` from its `LedgerSource`;
  - `cache` becomes `{ kind: "cache", x, y }` from its `LedgerCache`;
  - `player` becomes `{ kind: "carried", playerId }`;
  - `duel` becomes `{ kind: "duel", playerId }`.

Held types and claimed-out islands (islands with no sealed source left) follow from the rubbings, so they can't disagree with them. The ledger's sticky `freshRumors` flag isn't read. The config comes from `createIntelConfig({ preset, finalIsland, controlStartTick, map })`. The state comes from `createIntelState(config, seed)`, which starts before control start.

## Tests per branch

Each branch changed across the intel follow-ups has a deterministic test that fails when the branch is removed. Each mutation below is one line that still typechecks. Apply it on a scratch copy, then run `npx vitest run --project unit packages/simulation/src/intel packages/content/src/intel` (for 20, `npm run typecheck`), and the named test fails. ## Decisions taken here

- Held types and claimed-out islands are derived from the view's rubbings rather than passed separately.
- A pending sighting is one message per player holding a set of types, so two types that need a sighting at once are delivered together at the next boundary, not one interval apart, and the cap stays one sighting message per 30 s before minute 28.
- Every trigger of a step joins the step's set of (player, type) entries, with one sighting decision per player, so "learns about both at once" holds on every path: several losses, a loss with a replacement or a purchase, a batched view, and the boundary tick.
- A start points only at sources and caches. Sightings come only from a loss, a targeted rumor or a journal replacement.
- A free trigger that finds every copy carried but no snapshot entry to read yet waits like a capped one.
- A targeted request whose type a free trigger (or the start) of the same step gives the player is `covered` and not charged; the type goes out with the free reason. Of two requests for one (player, type) in one step, the first by id is charged and the other `covered`. Before, both were charged.
- Leads are decided in three phases (gather by (player, type), decide with keyed draws, answer grouped by (player, type)), so order independence holds by construction, and one player's purchase never changes another's result or draw.
- The state's `rng` is the seed of the keyed draws and no longer advances.
- After the minute-28 reveal a purchase of a carrier-only type is `covered`, since the broadcast is fresher; this is stateless, with no per-player memory. A purchase of a pending carrier-only type is `covered`, since the boundary gives it free. Both come from `freeCoverage`, shared by the step and the UI. A purchase with a source or cache target stays a charged rumor and drops a pending entry of its type at the next boundary.

# Encounters

§6's rules for starting and leaving duels, as pure code: `@pirate-sea-race/simulation/encounters` (`stepEncounters`), with the tuning in `@pirate-sea-race/content/encounters` (`encounterRules`, validated by `validateEncounterRules`). They decide who can attack whom, the telegraphed attempt and its escape, same-tick reservation, the ready check and the return to the world. They move no ship, run no duel and touch no inventory. The caller (the match room, `encounters-online`) does those things and reports back. Like `stepClaim`, `stepEncounters(config, state, input) → { state, events }` reads one tick's snapshot, never mutates its input, and uses only integers. Players, attempts and reports are read as sets, so their order in the input never matters.

## Attacks

| | Sea grapple (`ship`) | Island challenge (`foot`) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Windup | 20 ticks (1 s) | 12 ticks (0.6 s) |
| Range | 6 tiles (`ENGAGEMENT_RANGE_TILES`) | 2 tiles |
| Target cone at the start / hit area at landing | ±8 / ±4 headings | ±8 / ±4 headings |
| Line of sight | supercover line touching no land | placeholder: never blocked |
| Miss cooldown | 120 ticks (6 s) | 120 ticks (6 s) |

A press starts an attempt only if the rules find a target: the nearest eligible player of the same mode in range, in line of sight and in the ±8 front cone of the attacker's heading, ties to the lower id. Otherwise nothing happens and nothing is spent. The aim locks to the bearing toward the target. At the landing tick the attempt hits if the defender is still eligible, in range, within ±4 of the aim and in line of sight. Otherwise it misses, and the attacker's cooldown starts.

**Eligibility.** The attacker must be in the snapshot, connected, not in a duel, not respawning, out of cooldown and without an attempt already running. The defender must be in the snapshot (it may be disconnected, §12), in the same mode, not in a duel, not respawning and unprotected. Fewer than `maxDuels` (4) duels may be unsettled. An attacker who disconnects, leaves, changes mode or is reserved during the windup loses the attempt (`attempt-cancelled`, no cooldown). A defender who has become ineligible by the landing tick is a miss (`defender-ineligible`), as §6 says.

**Geometry**, defined once in `geometry.ts`. Positions are sub-units (256 a tile), and distances are compared squared: exactly at the range is in range. The *bearing* is the heading (of 64) whose table vector has the largest dot product with the offset, ties to the lower heading. *Within ±N* means a circular heading difference of at most N. Distance 0 has no bearing and is inside every cone. *Line of sight* (sea) is the supercover line between the centres of the two ships' tiles: every tile the segment touches, and both side tiles where it passes exactly through a corner. It is the same set in both directions. A land tile or a tile off the map blocks. Shoals and docks do not.

**Per-mode rules** (`ModeRules` in `modes.ts`: `lineOfSight`, `separateReturn`, `respawnPoint`) come from the config. `seaModeRules(map)` is complete. `footPlaceholderRules` never blocks line of sight and returns every player to where they stood. `objectives-endgame` replaces it through `createEncounterConfig({ modeRules: { foot } })`.

## State

`EncounterState` is plain data that `hashState` covers:

- `tick`: the last tick processed.
- `closed`: set when the caller reports the match over. The step then ignores every later input.
- `players`: records only for players with something to remember, sorted by id. Each has `protection` (`{ source: spawn | win | draw | respawn, endTick }`, protected while `tick < endTick`), `cooldownEndTick`, and `respawn` (a loser waiting out of the world until `respawnTick`).
- `attempts`: one per attacker, with `defenderId`, `mode`, `aim`, `startTick` and `landTick`. These are the telegraphs to draw.
- `duels`: every duel from reservation to settlement, in reservation order. Each has `id = duel:<tick>:<attacker id length>:<attacker>:<defender>`, `mode`, `players` (attacker, defender), each player's position at the hit, and the encounter position (their midpoint). `phase` is `transition`, `fighting` or `ended`, and the duel also holds `startTick` and `end`.

`duelMarkers(state)` gives other players what §6 allows: `{ x, y, startTick }` for each duel, with no id and no player names. Spawn protection comes from `createEncounterState(config, { tick, spawnProtected: ids })` (45 s, §2).

## One tick, and where the caller runs it

The room runs `stepEncounters` first in each world tick, **before `stepClaim`** (§5: accepted reservations first). It passes the previous tick's claim and ledger outcomes as `protectionEndedBy` (`claim` after a `protection-ended` from `stepClaim`, `collection` after a ledger collection start). A protection ended by an objective therefore reaches the encounter rules one tick (50 ms) late. This lag is accepted. Within the step:

1. **Match over** (`matchOver: true`): every attempt is cancelled (`match-over`), and the state closes.
2. **Protection** that has run out (`expired`), or that last tick's claim or collection ended, ends.
3. **Reports**, in a fixed order. An `end` report is accepted once per duel (`duel-ended`), in `transition` or `fighting`, with its tick between the reservation and now. A second end report, an unknown duel, a stranger as winner, a future tick or a settlement before the end each give `report-refused` and change nothing. A `settled` report removes the duel (`duel-settled`) and returns its players:
   - after a **win**, the winner goes back to their own position at the hit (`player-returned`, `win`, 8 s from the settlement tick). The loser is `player-respawning` until 15 s after the fight's *end* tick, or the settlement tick if that is later, so the theft choice doesn't lengthen the wait;
   - after a **draw or cancellation**, both players go to the centres of two distinct navigable tiles within 6 tiles of the encounter and at least 3 tiles apart (`player-returned`, `draw`, 8 s). The pair chosen is the one nearest to where each player stood, ties row-major.
4. **Respawns** that are due take place (`player-respawned`, `respawn`, 20 s). The loser goes to the dock nearest the encounter with no other player (except those still respawning) within `SIGHT_RADIUS_TILES`, ties by dock id. If every dock has an opponent that close, the loser goes to the dock farthest from its nearest opponent. The dock is chosen from positions on the respawn tick.
5. **Transitions.** A fight starts once the 3 s countdown is over and both clients report `ready` (`duel-started`). If a client is still not ready 10 s after the reservation, it forfeits (`duel-forfeited`, which ends the duel with that tick as its end tick). If both are still not ready, the duel is cancelled (`duel-cancelled`, §12's double forfeit).
6. **Attempts.** Attempts whose attacker is no longer eligible are cancelled. Every attempt landing on this tick is resolved at once. Misses come first. Hits are sorted by attacker-to-defender distance, then attacker id, then defender id. A hit reserves a duel (`duel-reserved`) if both of its players are still free and the cap allows another duel. If a player is already taken, the hit is `attempt-preempted` (`conflict`). If the cap is reached, the hit is `attempt-preempted` (`duel-cap`). Neither costs a cooldown. Pending attempts by players just reserved are cancelled.
7. **Presses** start attempts (`attempt-started`, with `protection-ended`/`attack` first if the attacker was protected). Targets are chosen from the state before any of this tick's starts, so a protected player who attacks on this tick becomes a target only from the next tick.

## Mapping onto the ledger and the claim

| Event or report | The caller does |
| --- | --- |
| `duel-reserved` | `reserveDuel({ duelId, players, tick })`. Pass `state.duels` as the claim's `encounters` (`{ id, playerIds: players }`). |
| `duel-forfeited` | `reportDuelResult({ duelId, tick, outcome: "win", winner })`. Do not send an `end` report back. |
| `duel-cancelled` | `reportDuelResult({ duelId, tick, outcome: "cancelled" })`. Do not send an `end` report back. |
| A fight that ran ends (or a player quits, or the server faults) | `reportDuelResult` with the result, and an `end` report (`win` + `winner`, `draw` or `cancelled`) with the tick it ended. |
| The ledger settles the duel (a draw or cancellation at once, a win at `chooseTheft` or `advanceLedger`) | A `settled` report with the ledger's settlement tick. |
| `player-returned`, `player-respawned` | Move the ship (or player) to `x, y`. `protection` is also the claim's `protected` flag. |
| `stepClaim` emits `protection-ended`, or the ledger starts a collection or a cache claim | Set `protectionEndedBy` next tick (`collection` for both ledger holds). |
| `stepClaim` emits `match-ended` (its `duel-ended-without-theft` ends running duels) | Set `matchOver: true` next tick. |

## In the match room (`encounters-online`)

`MatchRoom` runs the step each world tick, after sailing: every ship is a `ship` player, `attack` is the grapple button (J) latched since the last world step, `ready` is the fighter's `duel-ready`, and `connected` whether its client is there (a disconnected ship stays in the snapshot for its seat's 60 s, so it can be grappled, §12). `matchOver` is false until `objectives-endgame`.

Since `rubbings-theft` the room maps the rules onto the objective ledger as the table above says. Per world tick, in this order:

1. `advanceLedger`: choice windows that closed settle with the default theft.
2. The §12 timers, on the same tick: a fighter away from an unfinished duel for 10 s is forfeited in its machine; a disconnected player whose seat deadline has come is expired in the ledger (their rubbings into a cache at the dock `respawnPoint` would choose for them) and their ship leaves.
3. `stepEncounters`, with the reports: a fight that ended since the last tick is reported to the ledger (`reportDuelResult`, unless a player's quit or expiry already decided it there) and its `end` goes to the rules as the ledger recorded it; a `settled` report goes for each duel the ledger has settled, never before. A duel's players therefore return only after the settlement. `duel-reserved` calls `reserveDuel`; a ready-check `duel-forfeited` or `duel-cancelled` calls `reportDuelResult` and gets no `end` report back.
4. The ledger's holds: each connected player moored at a dock and holding E continues, starts or (without E, mooring or a target) cancels a collection or a cache claim. A hold that starts sets `protectionEndedBy: "collection"` for the next tick, so collecting or claiming ends protection (§2, §6) one tick (50 ms) late.

A theft choice (`choose-theft`) arrives between ticks and calls `chooseTheft` at the last processed tick; its settlement is reported on the next tick. Nobody starts with spawn protection, because a private match has no start of play yet. The room's own part (the duel machine, the returns, what each client may see) is in `docs/architecture.md` and `docs/duel.md`.

## Open points

- Island walking doesn't exist yet. The island challenge is tested for timing, range, cone and cooldown only, with caller-supplied positions.
- If a sea has no valid pair of draw points within 6 tiles, both ships stay where they were. The property tests check the spacing on every draw they produce.

Otherwise nothing happens and nothing is spent. The aim locks to the bearing toward the target. At the landing tick the attempt hits if the defender is still eligible, in range, within ±4 of the aim and in line of sight. Otherwise it misses, and the attacker's cooldown starts.

**Eligibility.** The attacker must be in the snapshot, connected, not in a duel, not respawning, out of cooldown and without an attempt already running. The defender must be in the snapshot (it may be disconnected, §12), in the same mode, not in a duel, not respawning and unprotected. Fewer than `maxDuels` (4) duels may be unsettled. An attacker who disconnects, leaves, changes mode or is reserved during the windup loses the attempt (`attempt-cancelled`, no cooldown). A defender who has become ineligible by the landing tick is a miss (`defender-ineligible`), as §6 says.

**Geometry**, defined once in `geometry.ts`. Positions are sub-units (256 a tile), and distances are compared squared: exactly at the range is in range. The *bearing* is the heading (of 64) whose table vector has the largest dot product with the offset, ties to the lower heading. *Within ±N* means a circular heading difference of at most N. Distance 0 has no bearing and is inside every cone. *Line of sight* (sea) is the supercover line between the centres of the two ships' tiles: every tile the segment touches, and both side tiles where it passes exactly through a corner. It is the same set in both directions. A land tile or a tile off the map blocks. Shoals and docks do not.

**Per-mode rules** (`ModeRules` in `modes.ts`: `lineOfSight`, `separateReturn`, `respawnPoint`) come from the config. `seaModeRules(map)` is complete. `footPlaceholderRules` never blocks line of sight and returns every player to where they stood. `objectives-endgame` replaces it through `createEncounterConfig({ modeRules: { foot } })`.

## State

`EncounterState` is plain data that `hashState` covers:

- `tick`: the last tick processed.
- `closed`: set when the caller reports the match over. The step then ignores every later input.
- `players`: records only for players with something to remember, sorted by id. Each has `protection` (`{ source: spawn | win | draw | respawn, endTick }`, protected while `tick < endTick`), `cooldownEndTick`, and `respawn` (a loser waiting out of the world until `respawnTick`).
- `attempts`: one per attacker, with `defenderId`, `mode`, `aim`, `startTick` and `landTick`. These are the telegraphs to draw.
- `duels`: every duel from reservation to settlement, in reservation order. Each has `id = duel:<tick>:<attacker id length>:<attacker>:<defender>`, `mode`, `players` (attacker, defender), each player's position at the hit, and the encounter position (their midpoint). `phase` is `transition`, `fighting` or `ended`, and the duel also holds `startTick` and `end`.

`duelMarkers(state)` gives other players what §6 allows: `{ x, y, startTick }` for each duel, with no id and no player names. Spawn protection comes from `createEncounterState(config, { tick, spawnProtected: ids })` (45 s, §2).

## One tick, and where the caller runs it

The room runs `stepEncounters` first in each world tick, **before `stepClaim`** (§5: accepted reservations first). It passes the previous tick's claim and ledger outcomes as `protectionEndedBy` (`claim` after a `protection-ended` from `stepClaim`, `collection` after a ledger collection start). A protection ended by an objective therefore reaches the encounter rules one tick (50 ms) late. This lag is accepted. Within the step:

1. **Match over** (`matchOver: true`): every attempt is cancelled (`match-over`), and the state closes.
2. **Protection** that has run out (`expired`), or that last tick's claim or collection ended, ends.
3. **Reports**, in a fixed order. An `end` report is accepted once per duel (`duel-ended`), in `transition` or `fighting`, with its tick between the reservation and now. A second end report, an unknown duel, a stranger as winner, a future tick or a settlement before the end each give `report-refused` and change nothing. A `settled` report removes the duel (`duel-settled`) and returns its players:
   - after a **win**, the winner goes back to their own position at the hit (`player-returned`, `win`, 8 s from the settlement tick). The loser is `player-respawning` until 15 s after the fight's *end* tick, or the settlement tick if that is later, so the theft choice doesn't lengthen the wait;
   - after a **draw or cancellation**, both players go to the centres of two distinct navigable tiles within 6 tiles of the encounter and at least 3 tiles apart (`player-returned`, `draw`, 8 s). The pair chosen is the one nearest to where each player stood, ties row-major.
4. **Respawns** that are due take place (`player-respawned`, `respawn`, 20 s). The loser goes to the dock nearest the encounter with no other player (except those still respawning) within `SIGHT_RADIUS_TILES`, ties by dock id. If every dock has an opponent that close, the loser goes to the dock farthest from its nearest opponent. The dock is chosen from positions on the respawn tick.
5. **Transitions.** A fight starts once the 3 s countdown is over and both clients report `ready` (`duel-started`). If a client is still not ready 10 s after the reservation, it forfeits (`duel-forfeited`, which ends the duel with that tick as its end tick). If both are still not ready, the duel is cancelled (`duel-cancelled`, §12's double forfeit).
6. **Attempts.** Attempts whose attacker is no longer eligible are cancelled. Every attempt landing on this tick is resolved at once. Misses come first. Hits are sorted by attacker-to-defender distance, then attacker id, then defender id. A hit reserves a duel (`duel-reserved`) if both of its players are still free and the cap allows another duel. If a player is already taken, the hit is `attempt-preempted` (`conflict`). If the cap is reached, the hit is `attempt-preempted` (`duel-cap`). Neither costs a cooldown. Pending attempts by players just reserved are cancelled.
7. **Presses** start attempts (`attempt-started`, with `protection-ended`/`attack` first if the attacker was protected). Targets are chosen from the state before any of this tick's starts, so a protected player who attacks on this tick becomes a target only from the next tick.

## Mapping onto the ledger and the claim

| Event or report | The caller does |
| --- | --- |
| `duel-reserved` | `reserveDuel({ duelId, players, tick })`. Pass `state.duels` as the claim's `encounters` (`{ id, playerIds: players }`). |
| `duel-forfeited` | `reportDuelResult({ duelId, tick, outcome: "win", winner })`. Do not send an `end` report back. |
| `duel-cancelled` | `reportDuelResult({ duelId, tick, outcome: "cancelled" })`. Do not send an `end` report back. |
| A fight that ran ends (or a player quits, or the server faults) | `reportDuelResult` with the result, and an `end` report (`win` + `winner`, `draw` or `cancelled`) with the tick it ended. |
| The ledger settles the duel (a draw or cancellation at once, a win at `chooseTheft` or `advanceLedger`) | A `settled` report with the ledger's settlement tick. |
| `player-returned`, `player-respawned` | Move the ship (or player) to `x, y`. `protection` is also the claim's `protected` flag. |
| `stepClaim` emits `protection-ended`, or the ledger starts a collection or a cache claim | Set `protectionEndedBy` next tick (`collection` for both ledger holds). |
| `stepClaim` emits `match-ended` (its `duel-ended-without-theft` ends running duels) | Set `matchOver: true` next tick. |

## In the match room (`encounters-online`)

`MatchRoom` runs the step each world tick, after sailing: every ship is a `ship` player, `attack` is the grapple button (J) latched since the last world step, `ready` is the fighter's `duel-ready`, and `connected` whether its client is there (a disconnected ship stays in the snapshot for its seat's 60 s, so it can be grappled, §12). `matchOver` is false until `objectives-endgame`.

Since `rubbings-theft` the room maps the rules onto the objective ledger as the table above says. Per world tick, in this order:

1. `advanceLedger`: choice windows that closed settle with the default theft.
2. The §12 timers, on the same tick: a fighter away from an unfinished duel for 10 s is forfeited in its machine; a disconnected player whose seat deadline has come is expired in the ledger (their rubbings into a cache at the dock `respawnPoint` would choose for them) and their ship leaves.
3. `stepEncounters`, with the reports: a fight that ended since the last tick is reported to the ledger (`reportDuelResult`, unless a player's quit or expiry already decided it there) and its `end` goes to the rules as the ledger recorded it; a `settled` report goes for each duel the ledger has settled, never before. A duel's players therefore return only after the settlement. `duel-reserved` calls `reserveDuel`; a ready-check `duel-forfeited` or `duel-cancelled` calls `reportDuelResult` and gets no `end` report back.
4. The ledger's holds: each connected player moored at a dock and holding E continues, starts or (without E, mooring or a target) cancels a collection or a cache claim. A hold that starts sets `protectionEndedBy: "collection"` for the next tick, so collecting or claiming ends protection (§2, §6) one tick (50 ms) late.

A theft choice (`choose-theft`) arrives between ticks and calls `chooseTheft` at the last processed tick; its settlement is reported on the next tick. Nobody starts with spawn protection, because a private match has no start of play yet. The room's own part (the duel machine, the returns, what each client may see) is in `docs/architecture.md` and `docs/duel.md`.

## Open points

- Island walking doesn't exist yet. The island challenge is tested for timing, range, cone and cooldown only, with caller-supplied positions.
- If a sea has no valid pair of draw points within 6 tiles, both ships stay where they were. The property tests check the spacing on every draw they produce.

*    latest two are kept.
 * 2. Per player, by id: the diff of held types resolves rumors for types gained; rumors whose target was emptied go
 *    stale; a completed or broken full set announces the final sector and sends or suspends the route.
 * 3. The leads, in three phases. Gather: every trigger joins a set keyed by (player, type): a type lost, a stale
 *    rumor's replacement, a pending type at a boundary, a targeted request. Decide: per player by id, a starting
 *    rumor first (never a sighting), then each entry in type order: a journal rumor, a no-lead, or its type joins the
 *    player's one sighting decision (one message listing every type the older snapshot can answer, or, capped, the free
 *    types wait as the one pending set); a purchase that `freeCoverage` covers sends nothing. Answer: each (player,
 *    type)'s requests by request id (`answerRequests`).
 * 4. The minute-20 sector reveal and the minute-28 carrier broadcasts, when their boundary was crossed.
 *
 * Every draw is keyed by (seed, tick, player, type), so no decision depends on the order of the triggers, requests or
 * view arrays. Boundaries fire when crossed since the last processed tick, so a skipped tick never loses one. Before
 * control start only the held types are tracked, and no message is sent. The input state is never mutated.
 */
export function stepIntel(
  config: IntelConfig,
  state: IntelState,
  view: IntelWorldView,
  requests: readonly TargetedRumorRequest[] = [],
): IntelStepResult {
  const world = readView(config, view, state.tick);
  for (const request of requests) {
    requireId(request.requestId, "request id");
    requireId(request.playerId, "request player id");
    if (typeof request.type !== "string") throw new RangeError(`request ${request.requestId} has no type`);

content.content:
# Pirate Sea Race

A browser multiplayer pirate treasure race. The game is specified in [`docs/spec.md`](docs/spec.md) (the text of `docs/spec.docx`); [`docs/architecture.md`](docs/architecture.md) maps this repository onto it.

Browsers create or join a private match by a six-character code and sail placeholder ships around the slice sea: a compact map with four small islands with docks, reefs and shoal walls that funnel every route between islands through one central crossing, and eight outer-sea spawn slots. Up (or W) sails ahead, down (S) brakes and then reverses, left and right (A, D) turn, and E docks a ship beside a dock, at any speed. The authoritative server decides every position and sends each browser only the ships within its sight radius; the minimap's fog clears where the player has sailed.

Fights happen at sea (§6): J grapples the nearest ship ahead within six tiles. The attacker sees its aim, the target a warning with the side it comes from, and it lands after a one-second windup unless the target sails out of range or out of the aim (a miss costs six seconds). A grapple that lands stops both ships; after a three-second countdown the two fight the online duel inside the match, in the same page's arena, while everyone else in sight sees crossed swords and the elapsed time where they fight. The winner sails on with eight seconds of protection; the loser respawns at a dock 15 seconds after the fight, with 20 seconds of protection; a draw returns both to separate nearby points.

The race is for rubbings (§4; the slice plays Sun and Moon, two sealed sources on each island). Moor at an island's dock and keep holding E: after six seconds you collect its rubbing of a type you lack (the HUD shows what the island holds, only while you are moored there, and the hold's progress). Win a duel at sea and, within five seconds, press 1 or 2 (or click) to steal one of the loser's types you lack, with 20 % of their gold (the rarest type is taken if you do not choose; a draw moves nothing). The purse beside the game shows your gold, your rubbings and what the last duel took or gave, and whether the winner chose it or the default took it. A player who drops keeps their seat, ship and rubbings for 60 seconds (a fighter away from a duel for ten seconds forfeits it); one who never returns, or quits, leaves a recovery cache at a dock, a chest others see when in sight. Moor there and hold E to claim one rubbing of a type you lack.

The standalone duel (the combat spike, §18 stage 1) runs beside it: "Create duel" makes a 1v1 duel whose code the second browser enters under "Join duel", and "Practice" fights a server-side dummy (idle or guarding). After a three-second countdown both browsers predict the fight with the shared duel simulation and roll back to the server's inputs (`docs/duel.md`). Keys (§8): WASD or the arrows move (hold back to guard), J light, K heavy, U and I specials, Shift dash, J and K together throw. The HUD shows both health bars, stamina, the round clock, the connection line (round trip, input delay, corrections) and the result; "Show hitboxes" draws hurtboxes and active hitboxes.

## Requirements

Node 24 and npm 11. The browser tests use Playwright's Chromium for `@playwright/test` 1.63.0, which must already be installed.

## Commands

Run these from the repository root.

| Task | Command |
| --- | --- |
| Install | `npm ci` |
| Develop (server on 2593, web on 5393, both from source) | `npm run dev` |
| Typecheck every workspace | `npm run typecheck` |
| Unit tests | `npm run test:unit` |
| Integration tests (a real server in-process, headless clients) | `npm run test:integration` |
| Build every package and the web client, then smoke-test the built server | `npm run build` |
| Convert the Tiled map `assets/source/maps/slice-sea.tmj` into `packages/content/src/maps/sliceSea.ts` (validated first) | `npm run map:build` |
| Check that the generated map module is up to date (a unit test checks this too) | `npm run map:check` |
| Run the built server | `npm start` |
| Browser tests (start the server and web client themselves) | `npx --no-install playwright test --config=tests/e2e/playwright.config.ts` |

Set `VITE_SERVER_URL` when the web client should reach a server other than port 2593 on its own host.

**Simulated latency for duel playtests (development only).** With `npm run dev`, add `?rtt=80&jitter=20` to the page's address (for example `http://localhost:5393/?rtt=80&jitter=20`) before creating or joining a duel: that browser's duel socket is then delayed by half the round trip each way, plus a uniform ±jitter/2, in order, round-trip probes included, so the HUD's round trip and the chosen input delay reflect it. Give both browsers the setting to test §19's 30, 80 or 150 ms. It is read only when `import.meta.env.DEV` is true and is absent from the production build (`npm run build` checks). Loss is simulated only by the test harness (`ImpairmentProxy` in `packages/test-tools`).

The map is generated from an ASCII sketch of one quarter, `assets/source/maps/sliceSeaSketch.ts`: edit it, then run `npm run map:build -- --from-sketch` (details in `assets/source/maps/README.md`). The `.tmj` stays within the Tiled subset documented in `packages/content/src/tiledMap.ts`, so [Tiled](https://www.mapeditor.org/) opens it.

`PIRATE_SEA_RACE_TEST_PLACEMENT=1` is a test-only setting, off by default: the dev and test entry point (`npm run dev`, and the server the browser tests start) then serves `POST /__test/place`, which puts a player's ship on a chosen tile. `PIRATE_SEA_RACE_TEST_SOURCES` (for example `sun,sun|moon,moon|sun,sun|moon,moon`, each island's source types) is another, off by default: every match then deals its rubbings in that layout instead of the private shuffle. The production entry (`npm start`) reads neither.

The integration tests run in two groups (`npm run test:integration`): most files in parallel worker processes, with test-only shorter timings, then the netcode harness files (`duelHarness`, `seaDuelHarness`, `devLatency`) one after another on a quiet machine.

## Layout

| Path | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| `apps/web` | Phaser client: landing page, HUD, input, interpolated rendering, the duel arena and HUD |
| `apps/server` | Colyseus match and duel server |
| `packages/simulation` | Pure fixed-step simulation shared by client and server, the duel and its rollback netcode |
| `packages/protocol` | Message schemas, validation and the protocol version |
| `packages/content` | The generated sea map, the Tiled converter, map validators, tuning, rules presets and frame budgets |
| `packages/test-tools` | Headless match and duel clients, the network impairment proxy and the duel replay wrapper |
| `tests/unit`, `tests/integration`, `tests/e2e` | Cross-package unit tests, server integration tests, Playwright scenarios |
| `assets/source/maps` | The Tiled source map and the sketch it is generated from |
| `assets/source`, `assets/exported`, `infra` | Placeholders for art sources, runtime assets and deployment |
3:The pure rubbing ledger of §4 with duel settlement (§11's theft and PvP gold), §12's recovery caches and §11's small match economy. `@pirate-sea-race/simulation/objectives` has the state, the operations and the invariant. `@pirate-sea-race/content/objectives` has the types, rubbing ids, timings, the gold and economy rules and the zod validators for source sites and assignments. It is plain integer data with no clocks and no `Math.random`. Time is the world tick (20 per second), supplied by the caller. Positions are integer sub-units, supplied by the caller. `MatchRoom` runs it since `rubbings-theft` (below, and `docs/architecture.md`).
9:- **Sources:** `assignSources(preset, sites, seed)` deals the rubbings onto the caller's sites with a seeded Fisher–Yates shuffle. There must be `sourcesPerIsland` sites per island. Source ids are `source-<island>-<slot>`. `sourceAssignmentSchema` checks the result: each rubbing sealed once, the right island counts, unique ids, and types that match the ids.
98:The tests run every operation on a deeply frozen state and check the invariant after each one. The property tests run 3 seeded matches per preset, 1200 random steps each, about 2700–5100 operations each. The steps cover:
106:- from a second seeded stream between those steps, so the match around them is unchanged: ruin and supply grants (repeated keys included), purchases (request ids shared between players, retried purchases and refusals, and a player's id reused for the other item included) and tonic use.
108:After every step they also check the gold identity, non-negative gold and the tonic count directly, and that a tonic only activates when none was active for that player. A rejected step must return its input state, except a purchase refusal decided for the first time, which may only add itself to `requests`. The same seed replays to the same `hashState`.
122:- **One ledger per match**, the `slice` preset, seeded from the room's own private randomness (never the public match code). Its sites are each regular island's docks, `sourcesPerIsland` (2) per island in dock id order, reusing a dock when an island has fewer (`apps/server/src/objectives.ts`). **Until the ruins are wired (`objectives-endgame`), every source is unlocked at match start**; the ruins feature will lock them behind its puzzles.

The standalone duel (the combat spike, §18 stage 1) runs beside it: "Create duel" makes a 1v1 duel whose code the second browser enters under "Join duel", and "Practice" fights a server-side dummy (idle or guarding). After a three-second countdown both browsers predict the fight with the shared duel simulation and roll back to the server's inputs (`docs/duel.md`). Keys (§8): WASD or the arrows move (hold back to guard), J light, K heavy, U and I specials, Shift dash, J and K together throw. The HUD shows both health bars, stamina, the round clock, the connection line (round trip, input delay, corrections) and the result; "Show hitboxes" draws hurtboxes and active hitboxes.

## Requirements

Node 24 and npm 11. The browser tests use Playwright's Chromium for `@playwright/test` 1.63.0, which must already be installed.

## Commands

Run these from the repository root.

| Task | Command |
| --- | --- |
| Install | `npm ci` |
| Develop (server on 2593, web on 5393, both from source) | `npm run dev` |
| Typecheck every workspace | `npm run typecheck` |
| Unit tests | `npm run test:unit` |
| Integration tests (a real server in-process, headless clients) | `npm run test:integration` |
| Build every package and the web client, then smoke-test the built server | `npm run build` |
| Convert the Tiled map `assets/source/maps/slice-sea.tmj` into `packages/content/src/maps/sliceSea.ts` (validated first) | `npm run map:build` |
| Check that the generated map module is up to date (a unit test checks this too) | `npm run map:check` |
| Run the built server | `npm start` |
| Browser tests (start the server and web client themselves) | `npx --no-install playwright test --config=tests/e2e/playwright.config.ts` |

Set `VITE_SERVER_URL` when the web client should reach a server other than port 2593 on its own host.

**Simulated latency for duel playtests (development only).** With `npm run dev`, add `?rtt=80&jitter=20` to the page's address (for example `http://localhost:5393/?rtt=80&jitter=20`) before creating or joining a duel: that browser's duel socket is then delayed by half the round trip each way, plus a uniform ±jitter/2, in order, round-trip probes included, so the HUD's round trip and the chosen input delay reflect it. Give both browsers the setting to test §19's 30, 80 or 150 ms. It is read only when `import.meta.env.DEV` is true and is absent from the production build (`npm run build` checks). Loss is simulated only by the test harness (`ImpairmentProxy` in `packages/test-tools`).

The map is generated from an ASCII sketch of one quarter, `assets/source/maps/sliceSeaSketch.ts`: edit it, then run `npm run map:build -- --from-sketch` (details in `assets/source/maps/README.md`). The `.tmj` stays within the Tiled subset documented in `packages/content/src/tiledMap.ts`, so [Tiled](https://www.mapeditor.org/) opens it.

`PIRATE_SEA_RACE_TEST_PLACEMENT=1` is a test-only setting, off by default: the dev and test entry point (`npm run dev`, and the server the browser tests start) then serves `POST /__test/place`, which puts a player's ship on a chosen tile. `PIRATE_SEA_RACE_TEST_SOURCES` (for example `sun,sun|moon,moon|sun,sun|moon,moon`, each island's source types) is another, off by default: every match then deals its rubbings in that layout instead of the private shuffle. The production entry (`npm start`) reads neither.

The integration tests run in two groups (`npm run test:integration`): most files in parallel worker processes, with test-only shorter timings, then the netcode harness files (`duelHarness`, `seaDuelHarness`, `devLatency`) one after another on a quiet machine.

- **Rumor flow:** the room first asks the intel module whether a targeted rumor is available for the player (a missing type with a lead). Only then does it call `purchase` with the client's request id. On `ok && !replayed` it asks intel to deliver the rumor under that (player, request id). On `ok && replayed` it resends the rumor already delivered. On `!ok` (`replayed` or not) it sends the refusal and delivers nothing: a `replayed` refusal is the original answer, so a delayed retry never buys what the player was refused. A rumor that cannot be delivered is never bought.

## In the match room (`rubbings-theft`)

- **One ledger per match**, the `slice` preset, seeded from the room's own private randomness (never the public match code). Its sites are each regular island's docks, `sourcesPerIsland` (2) per island in dock id order, reusing a dock when an island has fewer (`apps/server/src/objectives.ts`). **Until the ruins are wired (`objectives-endgame`), every source is unlocked at match start**; the ruins feature will lock them behind its puzzles.
- **Holding E** moored at a dock of island *i* works on its first eligible target: the island's sealed, unlocked source of a type the player lacks, else a rubbing of a type they lack in a recovery cache at that dock, each in the fixed type order. The room calls `startCollect`/`startCacheClaim`, then `progressChannel` every held tick, and `cancelChannel` when E is released, the ship casts off or the target is gone. A reservation (`reserveDuel`) and a disconnect cancel it inside the ledger.
- **Duels** follow `docs/encounters.md`'s mapping; the room reports `settled` to the rules only once the ledger has settled.
- **§12** runs on the world tick: `disconnectPlayer` at a drop, `reconnectPlayer` on return, `expireReservation` at the deadline (the cache at the dock the rules would respawn the player at), `quitPlayer` for every other leave (the cache at the dock nearest the ship by sea).
- **The room asserts `checkLedger`** after every world tick in development and tests, together with its own invariant (no ship removed while the ledger counts its player in the match).
- **Test-only settings** (never read by the production entry): `startGameServer({ matchTuning })` overrides the rules (for example a short seat reservation) and pins the source layout; the dev entry reads `PIRATE_SEA_RACE_TEST_SOURCES`.

## Decisions taken here

- The slice uses Sun and Moon.
- "Free sources" in the default theft counts sealed sources, locked or not. Cached rubbings are not counted.
- The repeated-win window is measured from the previous win over that opponent, whether or not that win paid gold.
- A winner who leaves during the choice window takes nothing.
- Both players leaving a fight on the same tick cancel it, in either order. The ledger cannot rely on processing order (§7), so a forfeit waits one tick before it can commit.
- Both players stay reserved until the choice window settles, so neither can collect or be challenged during it.
- Economy grants and purchases check whether the player has left. Grants ignore duels and disconnects, because the reward was earned before. Purchases and tonics refuse disconnected players, as channels do.
- A repeated purchase id is looked up before the tick check, so a retry still finds its purchase or refusal after the clock moved on.
- Kept refusals are bounded (16 per player, oldest evicted) so a client cannot grow the state without limit; purchases are bounded by gold.
- Every purse is the rules' `startingGold`; tests that need other purses change that rule for the whole ledger.

No empty stretches: every navigable tile is within the sight radius of land, a shoal or a dock (not the edge). Routes meet: closing the disc around the hub (open sea near the centre; radius half the sight radius, so ships in it see each other) lengthens or cuts every shortest path between docks of different islands. At most 112 tiles a side. The slice sea (111 × 111 tiles, midline shoal walls open only in the hub's disc): neighbours 26 s apart, longest crossing 39 s, water within 9.9 tiles of an obstacle, 90 % open sea.

-- **Final-island sockets (§3, §5).** `map.finalSockets` holds four identical dockless islets (one sketched islet, mirrored), each a rectangle of at most 6 × 6 and a claim tile: open sea beside it whose centre is the claim point, the treasure circle's centre (`TREASURE_CIRCLE_RADIUS_TILES`). - **Sailing.** Positions are integer sub-units (256 a tile); headings are 64 directions, 0 east, clockwise (y grows down), unit vectors from a literal cosine table. Each world step the throttle (`-moveY`) accelerates towards 39 sub-units a step (3.05 tiles a second), brakes, or reverses slowly from a stop; `moveX` turns a heading a step (3.2 s a circle); none coasts to a stop. On 24 px tiles that handles like the old five tiles a second on 16 px (unit tests hold it within 25 %). The hull is a square of half-size 80. A move sweeps each axis in turn through the tile columns or rows its leading edge enters and stops flush at the first land, shoal or map edge: a ship slides along an obstacle met at an angle, runs aground head-on, and never tunnels.

- **Docking.** Hold E near a dock to moor, at any speed and throttle: with the hull on or beside the berth tile (unless pinched), or within reach with a clear run, it moves to the dock's centre, stops and records the dock, so no arrival slides past or grounds beside it (pinched: a diagonal tile whose two shared tiles are blocked). It stays moored while E or the throttle it moored with (`mooredThrottle`) is held; pressing a throttle after releasing that one, or the other direction, casts off. An input stall does not: the server gives a lapsed client no input, keeping the latch. The keyboard keeps a tap of E until its next read (not past a blur), the server until its next step; then the HUD says "Press E to dock".

- **Visibility boundary (§16).** The room's `ships` map is tagged `.view()`. Each client gets a `StateView`; after every mirror the room puts into it the client's own ship and each ship within `SIGHT_RADIUS_TILES` (10, `visibleShipIds`) and takes out the rest, so Colyseus encodes no other ship into that client's patches (an integration test checks the decoded state and the raw frames). `players` in the state is the public player count. Terrain is static content every client bundles, never synced; the minimap fog is client-side presentation, not a security boundary.

It only moves a ship: admission and views are unchanged.

+- **Test-only timings and source layout.** `startGameServer({ matchTuning })` gives every match of that server other rules (a short seat reservation, respawn wait, duel absence, ready countdown, protection, match, channel or reveals), a pinned source layout, a pinned final-socket secret, an injected master secret, or the room's test hooks; integration tests use it and assert in world ticks. Colyseus has one matchmaker per process, so each integration test file has one set of timings. The dev and test entry also reads `PIRATE_SEA_RACE_TEST_SOURCES` (for example `sun,sun|moon,moon|sun,sun|moon,moon`: the types of each island's sources), `PIRATE_SEA_RACE_TEST_TIMINGS` (for example `ready=60,protection=20,match=12000`, in world ticks; also `sectors` and `carriers`) and `PIRATE_SEA_RACE_TEST_FINAL_SECRET` (a 32-bit secret), which the browser tests set so a scenario picks an island by type, plays a whole match in a minute and knows where the treasure is. All are off by default. `main.ts` reads none (the build smoke test starts it with all of them set, malformed, and checks the 20 s countdown and 35:00 timer) and turns the per-tick invariant checks off.

-- **Encounters in the room.** Each world step (20 Hz), after sailing, `MatchRoom` builds one tick's snapshot for `stepEncounters` (`docs/encounters.md`): every ship's position and heading, whether its player is connected, pressed J since the last world step (the input gate latches it like E), has a loaded arena, or started a collection or cache claim last tick (which ends protection). It passes back the reports of duels that ended since the last tick, and a settlement only once the ledger has settled the duel (below). It applies the events: `duel-reserved` stops both ships and opens a duel; `duel-started` starts its fight; a ready-check `duel-forfeited` or `duel-cancelled` ends it; `player-returned` and `player-respawned` move a ship (at rest, or moored at the dock). Everything else (attempts, protection, cooldowns, the loser's wait) is mirrored from the rules' state. The rules alone choose targets and decide hits, returns and docks; the room never re-implements them. Reserved and respawning ships get neutral input, so they stay put. Departure protection needs a match start, which private matches do not have yet, so no one starts protected.

Everything else (attempts, protection, cooldowns, the loser's wait) is mirrored from the rules' state. The rules alone choose targets and decide hits, returns and docks; the room never re-implements them. Reserved and respawning ships get neutral input, so they stay put. The rules run from control start, when every ship gets the departure's protection, to the match's end.

- **One duel machine.** `DuelMachine` (`apps/server/src/duelMachine.ts`) is the duel both rooms run: seats and their `DuelInputGate`s, the 180-frame countdown with round-trip probes and the input delay chosen 30 frames before its end, `DuelAuthority` stepped at 60 Hz with a bundle every third frame, the reconnection bookkeeping (a dropped seat is marked away, a returning one gets a snapshot bundle) and the forfeits decided together at the next frame boundary. It writes a lobby schema and sends through a callback, so the host room owns clients and timers. `DuelRoom` starts the fight when the countdown ends (`start: "countdown"`); the match room starts it when the rules say so (`start: "called"`: the countdown is over and both fighters sent `duel-ready`). A countdown that ends with a fighter still loading waits in `waiting`, without probes; clients drop their session then, so the fight's clock starts from the fight's own frames. The match room keeps each duel's lobby for 2 s after settlement (`DUEL_RESULT_TICKS`), so both read the result.

- **Absence** (§12, on the world tick). A drop anywhere disconnects the player in the ledger at once; the ship stays in the world, grapplable, for the 60 s seat reservation. A fighter away from an unfinished duel for 10 s, counted in world ticks, forfeits it (both on one frame: no winner, reported as cancelled) and respawns as any loser, keeping the seat. Back before the deadline, the same player continues (`reconnectPlayer`; a fighter gets a snapshot bundle). Colyseus' `allowReconnection` is only an outer bound (70 s) that keeps the socket's slot: at the ledger's deadline the room expires the reservation and releases that slot; any other leave (consented, or the outer bound first) is a quit.

- **Message routing.** A duel's `duel-frames` and `duel-probe` go to its two fighters only, with `client.send`; the room routes `duel-input`, `duel-probe` echoes and `duel-ready` from a session to that session's duel and drops them from anyone else. In the browser, `SeaDuelRouter` listens for the duel messages once per match and hands them to the duel client of the moment (a message that beats the lobby's patch waits for it); the same `DuelClient` runs a standalone duel over `duelRoomTransport`.

-- **The ledger per match.** `MatchRoom` creates a `slice` ledger with the match, seeded from its own private randomness (`MatchTuning.random`: `node:crypto`'s `randomInt` in production, never the public match code; tests inject their own source through `startGameServer({ matchTuning })` and show the deal follows it, `tests/integration/ledgerSeed.test.ts`). Its sources stand at each regular island's docks (two per island, in dock id order), all unlocked until the ruins are wired (`objectives-endgame` will lock them). The ledger is the only writer of rubbings and gold: the room calls its operations and never moves either itself, and after every world tick it checks `checkLedger` and its own invariant (every player the ledger counts in the match has a ship, and every ship such a player) in development and tests.

+- **The ledger per match.** `MatchRoom` creates a `slice` ledger with the match, seeded with the ledger's seed derived from the match's master secret (below). Its sources stand at each regular island's docks (two per island, in dock id order), all unlocked until the ruins are wired (`objectives-endgame` will lock them). The ledger is the only writer of rubbings and gold: the room calls its operations and never moves either itself, and after every world tick it checks `checkLedger` and its own invariant (every player the ledger counts in the match has a ship, and every ship such a player) in development and tests.

- **Collecting and claiming.** Holding E moored at a dock is one gesture: E moors, and the same hold works on E's target there, the island's first sealed source of a type the player lacks, else a cached rubbing of a type they lack (fixed type order). The room continues the ledger's hold every held tick; releasing E, casting off, a reservation or a disconnect cancels it, and progress resets. Starting a hold ends protection on the next tick.

- **Settlement order.** Each world tick: `advanceLedger` (a closed choice window settles with the default); the §12 timers (duel absence, seat expiry into a cache at the respawn dock); `stepEncounters`, whose reports tell the ledger a fight's result and the rules its end, and tell the rules `settled` only once the ledger has settled the duel; then the holds. On a win with an eligible type the winner gets 5 s to send `choose-theft`; a draw, a cancellation or a win with nothing to take settles at once (gold still moves on a win). Only then do the players return. The fighters' lobby stays in their views through the choice. Both fighters' notices carry the settlement's tick, who picked the stolen type (`settledChoice`: the winner, or the default at the deadline) and the choice's deadline tick, so the purse says "You chose Moon" (the loser: "They chose Moon") or "Taken by default: Moon". The web client maps a key (1, 2) or a click on option *n* to a type in one pure function (`chosenTheftType`, `hud.ts`) before it sends `choose-theft`.

- **Messages.** `choose-theft` `{ duel, type }` (protocol v6): the opaque key of the sender's own duel lobby and a rubbing type, zod-validated, at most 64 bytes and 8 a second; the ledger accepts it only from the winner, inside the window, for an eligible type, and otherwise changes nothing. Collecting and claiming need no message: E is the input's interact button.

- **What each client sees (§16).** Gold, rubbings, the hold and its progress, the last results and the theft options are in the player's own `status` entry only. The island's sealed types and a cache's contents are filled in only while the player is moored at that island's dock or that cache's dock. A cache is a contentless marker at its dock, in a view within the sight radius. Integration tests check raw frames: an onlooker in sight of a collection and a duel never receives a rubbing type at all.

- **Leaving.** A reservation that expires removes the player and puts their remaining rubbings in one cache at the dock the encounter rules would respawn them at; a quit (or Colyseus' outer bound) forfeits a duel in progress and caches the rest at the dock nearest the ship by sea (`seaPathCosts`). No path removes a ship while the ledger still counts its player. A cache never despawns; claimed empty, it disappears.

+- **Lobby.** A private match opens in its lobby (`phase` in the synced state). Its players are listed by seat ("Player 2": join order from 1; the state names players by seat, never by session id, so a ship's id still first reaches a client when it comes into sight, §16). The first joiner hosts (the host passes on when they leave). The host's `start-match` (zod-validated, empty, 4 a second) goes to the match module's `stepMatch`, which starts the ready countdown with 2 or more players present (`PRIVATE_MIN_PLAYERS`, the single source: the content's `privateMatch.minPlayers` of 1 is stale and not read) and otherwise answers `start-refused` (`too-few`, `not-host`). From the countdown on, the listing's metadata says `started` and admission refuses every join with "That match has already started" (the room's `onJoin` refuses too); if the countdown falls back to the lobby (fewer than 2 left), joins reopen. Ships are held (neutral input) until control starts and again after the end.

+- **Ready and departure.** The countdown lasts `readyTicks` (20 s) while clients preload (the arena scene is already in the page's one game). The flow's `control-started` tick starts everything that counts from it: the encounter rules' state with every ship protected for `spawnProtectionTicks` (45 s, which is also the departure's length), the claim config (`createClaimConfig`, its `deadlineTick` = control start + `deadlineTicks`), and the intel config and state. The timer the HUD shows is the match module's `remaining`, whose duration is the claim rules' `deadlineTicks`: both configs are built from one set of rules (`matchConfigFor`, `claimConfigFor` in `matchFlow.ts`), and a unit test and an integration test hold them equal.

+- **Tick order** (each world tick while the match runs): `advanceLedger` (closed theft windows), the §12 timers, then §5's order: **encounters** (accepted reservations first) → the ledger's holds → **claim** channel (`stepClaim`: every ship with `holdsAllTypes` from the ledger, E, speed, connection, protection, and the encounter rules' reserved duels) → **match flow** (`stepMatch`: the joins, leaves and starts since the last tick, this tick's accomplishments, and the claim's `match-ended`) → **intel reveals** (`stepIntel`). Before control start only the timers and the flow run. The room drops reports naming a player the flow does not know before calling `stepMatch`, which throws on them.

+- **Reveals.** The intel module reads the ledger's rubbings and the ships each tick; the room delivers only its reveal messages (rumors and the journal come with `intel-online`), each to exactly its recipients as `reveal` messages: `final-sector` to everyone at the first full set (also kept in the public state, name and index only), `final-route` with the exact claim point only to a full-set holder (also in that player's own status, with `routeActive`), `final-route-inactive` to a holder who lost a type, `sector-reveal` at minute 20 and `carrier-report` from minute 28 to everyone. An integration test checks raw frames: the other player never receives a `final-route`. The browser shows each as a banner and in a list; the holder gets a compass line, an arrow off the ship, the treasure circle and a minimap mark.

+- **The claim.** Stopped inside the treasure circle, holding every type and E, unreserved: the claim module's channel runs for `channelTicks` (10 s); starting it ends protection (the encounter rules hear it on the next tick). The player's status carries the channel's progress and the last reset's reason (moved, released, a duel, a lost type, a disconnect); the claim panel shows them with "Any rival in range can interrupt you with a grapple". Ships channelling show it to whoever sees them (a gold ring), and those players are warned. On `match-ended` the flow ends the match: outcomes freeze (a running duel is cancelled without theft, no ship takes input, nothing more is stepped).

+- **Endings and results.** `claim` (a winner), `deadline` (no winner; a claim completing on the deadline tick wins), `abandoned` (everyone left after the lobby; stepped once more as the room closes) and `aborted` (a world tick that throws is caught as §12's server fault). The accomplishments come from the ledger (`docs/objectives.md`) and settled duels. The results (the flow's) are synced to everyone once, shown until players leave (Back to lobby returns to the landing page), and recorded in the process's outcome list (`recordedOutcomes`).

+- **Seeds.** One private master secret per match (32 bytes of `node:crypto`'s `randomBytes`). Each system's seed is `HMAC-SHA-256(secret, "pirate-sea-race/seed/v1/" + system)`, its first four bytes: `world`, `ledger`, `final-socket`, `intel`, each duel's `duel:<n>`, and `ruins` and `fruit` reserved. No raw seed feeds two systems and none reads the match code; unit and integration tests check both.

+- **Test hooks** (`MatchTuning.testHooks`, off by default, never set by an entry point): `injectFault()` makes the next world tick throw (an `aborted` ending), and `pauseAfterTick(tick)` / `resumeWorld()` stop the clock after a tick so a test lines an input up with an exact tick (a grapple landing on a claim's completion tick, a claim completing on the deadline tick).

- **Duel room.** `DuelRoom` (room name `duel`) holds one duel, a `DuelMachine`: two players, or one in practice against a server-side dummy (player two, `idle` or `guard`). It is admitted like a match, by the same code in `admission.ts`: a one-time create token, `onAuth` before any seat, the room's own check, `filterBy(['code', 'createToken'])`, no token in the listing. The countdown (180 frames) starts once every seat is taken; the machine probes round trips during it, chooses the shared input delay 30 frames before the end, then steps `DuelAuthority` at 60 Hz, which the room's `setFixedTimestep` drives. Inputs go through `DuelInputGate`, which admits them through the same `InputAdmission` as the world's `InputGate` (the rate window and the protocol validation: 128 bytes, 60 a second of room ticks, increasing sequence, 30 frames of lead), so the two cannot drift, and counts its drops. Frame bundles and probes are Colyseus messages; the lobby is a small Schema state. A drop keeps the seat for 10 s (`allowReconnection`); leaving, or staying away, forfeits, decided at the next frame boundary (two forfeits on one frame: no winner). The rules and rates are in `docs/duel.md`.
